 How to Compare Medicare Part D Plans for 2027
 A practical guide to checking covered prescriptions, pharmacy prices and total yearly costs before Medicare Open Enrollment ends December 7.
 By: Daniel Brooks 
 | 
 Editor: Matthew Reed 
 November 8, 2026, 08:30 WITA · 4 min read 
 Archive photo: Prescription pills and capsules photographed in 1982. The image illustrates drug coverage and does not represent a specific Medicare formulary. 
 WASHINGTON, Aktualita.co — Medicare beneficiaries comparing prescription drug coverage for 2027 have until December 7 to make changes during fall Open Enrollment. A useful starting point is to enter every regular prescription and the pharmacies they use in Medicare Plan Compare, then compare estimated yearly costs before choosing a plan.
 The monthly premium is only one part of that decision. A plan with a lower premium could cost more overall if it charges more for a drug someone takes every month or treats the nearest pharmacy as a higher-cost option. Changes made during the October 15 to December 7 enrollment window take effect January 1, 2027, if the plan receives the request by the deadline.
 Advertisement 
 Start with your prescriptions and pharmacies
 Use a current medication list that includes drug names, doses, quantities and how often each prescription is filled. In Plan Compare, set the coverage year to 2027 and use the ZIP code where you live. Include your regular pharmacy and any practical alternatives so the estimates reflect where you could actually pick up refills.
 Medicare advises beneficiaries who are comparing plans:
 “Add all the prescription drugs you take regularly to get the most accurate monthly and yearly cost estimate for each plan.”
 Open the details for each plan and check its formulary, the list of drugs it covers. Look at the tier assigned to each prescription and whether the plan lists restrictions such as prior authorization, step therapy or quantity limits. If a prescription does not appear as expected, confirm the drug name and dose, then ask the plan about its coverage before relying on the estimate.
 Check pharmacy status as well. A location can be in a plan’s network without offering its lowest cost sharing. Compare the prices at nearby pharmacies you can use consistently, and consider mail delivery if the plan offers it and it suits your needs.
 Compare yearly cost and the timing of bills
 Compare the annual premium plus estimated drug spending at the pharmacy. Medicare.gov lists a maximum Part D deductible of $700 for 2027, up from $615 in 2026. Some plans charge less or no deductible. Check how the deductible applies to your prescriptions and whether you would face a larger bill early in the year.
 The 2027 out-of-pocket limit for covered Part D drugs is $2,400, compared with $2,100 in 2026. Once qualifying spending reaches the limit, beneficiaries pay nothing out of pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of that calendar year. Premiums are separate. The limit also does not cap all medical expenses or make a drug that is excluded from the plan’s coverage free.
 For a simple illustration, suppose one plan charges $15 a month and its estimated annual drug cost is $720. The combined estimate is $900. A second plan charging $35 a month with estimated annual drug costs of $360 totals $780. The second plan costs $120 less in this example, even though its premium is higher. These figures are hypothetical; check what each displayed estimate already includes so you do not count a deductible twice.
 Review your current coverage before switching
 Read your plan’s Annual Notice of Change alongside the comparison results. It can help you identify changes in premiums and cost sharing. Confirm that the formulary and pharmacy information you are reviewing applies to 2027. The lowest estimated total is useful only if the plan covers the medicines you need and its pharmacy options are practical.
 People with Original Medicare can compare stand-alone Part D plans. If you have Medicare Advantage, check how drug coverage is included and confirm with Medicare or the plan before joining a separate drug plan. A change to drug coverage may affect the health coverage you already have, so review the medical network and other costs as well.
 Beneficiaries who qualify for Extra Help may pay less for prescriptions. The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan serves a different purpose: it spreads eligible out-of-pocket costs across the calendar year without reducing the amount owed. It can help with the timing of bills if your costs are concentrated early in the year.
 Before submitting a change, record the plan name, its annual cost estimate and the pharmacy used for the comparison. Check that the plan will receive your request by December 7, and keep the enrollment confirmation for January. If you keep your current coverage, save its 2027 terms so you know what to expect at the first refill.
